Footmen
FUUT-men
n. pl.
From foot and men: soldiers who serve on foot, as distinguished from cavalry; also, runners or attendants. Webster 1828: soldiers who march and fight on foot. Jeremiah uses them as the measure of the easier trial.

Biblical Definition

The LORD’s answer to Jeremiah’s complaint is not comfort but a question, and it is one of the most bracing verses in the prophets: If thou hast run with the footmen, and they have wearied thee, then how canst thou contend with horses? and if in the land of peace, wherein thou trustedst, they wearied thee, then how wilt thou do in the swelling of Jordan? (Jeremiah 12:5). Jeremiah had asked why the wicked prosper; God replies that harder things are coming and that the present trouble is the lesser race. The word is a military one, denoting infantry as against cavalry. Moses uses it to count the nation: The people, among whom I am, are six hundred thousand footmen; and thou hast said, I will give them flesh, that they may eat a whole month (Numbers 11:21) — the arithmetic of unbelief, offered to God as an objection. And in one of the darkest scenes in Samuel, the king’s footmen refuse an order: the king said unto the footmen that stood about him, Turn, and slay the priests of the LORD... But the servants of the king would not put forth their hand to fall upon the priests of the LORD (1 Samuel 22:17).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines FOOTMAN as a soldier who marches and fights on foot; also a runner, or a menial servant who attends on foot; in the plural, infantry.

FOOTMAN, n. (pl. FOOTMEN) — A soldier who marches and fights on foot.

A runner; one who attends on foot.

A menial servant; a male attendant.

In the plural, infantry, as distinguished from horsemen or cavalry.

From foot and man.

Key Scripture

Jeremiah 12:5 — "If thou hast run with the footmen, and they have wearied thee, then how canst thou contend with horses? and if in the land of peace, wherein thou trustedst, they wearied thee, then how wilt thou do in the swelling of Jordan?"

Numbers 11:21 — "And Moses said, The people, among whom I am, are six hundred thousand footmen; and thou hast said, I will give them flesh, that they may eat a whole month."

1 Samuel 22:17 — "And the king said unto the footmen that stood about him, Turn, and slay the priests of the LORD; because their hand also is with David, and because they knew when he fled, and did not shew it to me. But the servants of the king would not put forth their hand to fall upon the priests of the LORD."

Jeremiah 12:1 — "Righteous art thou, O LORD, when I plead with thee: yet let me talk with thee of thy judgments: Wherefore doth the way of the wicked prosper? wherefore are all they happy that deal very treacherously?"

Modern Corruption

God’s reply to Jeremiah’s complaint is not consolation but a warning of harder trials, which contradicts the pastoral assumption that God’s answer to a struggling servant is always relief.

expand to see more

Jeremiah asks the oldest question — why the wicked prosper — and receives an answer no modern pastoral manual would recommend: If thou hast run with the footmen, and they have wearied thee, then how canst thou contend with horses? God does not explain the prosperity of the wicked, does not promise relief, and does not soften the coming difficulty. He tells His prophet that this was the easy part. The therapeutic assumption that a struggling believer must first be reassured cannot accommodate the verse, and it is worth noticing that Jeremiah was not thereby crushed: he went on to a ministry of forty years and to the book of Lamentations. God’s honesty about what was coming was itself a mercy, and preparing a servant is a different kind of kindness from comforting him.

1 Samuel 22:17 records one of Scripture’s clearest instances of lawful disobedience to a superior. Saul, the anointed king, commands his footmen to kill the priests of the LORD, and they refuse — and the narrative does not censure them. It was Doeg the Edomite who obeyed, and eighty-five priests died. The episode establishes what Romans 13 assumes and Acts 5:29 states: obedience to authority is owed within the bounds of God’s law and stops where a magistrate commands sin. The footmen had no office and no standing; they simply would not put forth their hand. The Reformed doctrine of the lesser magistrate develops the case of resistance through subordinate authority, but this passage shows the simpler duty that lies beneath it, which belongs to any man asked to do murder.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew ragli (H7273), one on foot, a footman; ruts (H7323), to run; parash (H6571), a horseman; the contrast in Jeremiah 12:5 is between infantry and cavalry.

expand to see more

Hebrew ragli (H7273) — on foot, a footman; from regel, the foot (Jeremiah 12:5; Numbers 11:21).

Hebrew ruts (H7323) — to run; if thou hast run with the footmen (Jeremiah 12:5).

Hebrew sus (H5483) — a horse; the harder contest of the same verse.

Hebrew gaon (H1347) — swelling, majesty, pride; the swelling of Jordan, the flooded thickets where lions lodged.

Hebrew ruts in 1 Samuel 22:17 — the king’s runners or guard, rendered footmen.

Usage

"If thou hast run with the footmen, and they have wearied thee (Jeremiah 12:5) — God tells His prophet this was the easy part."

"Six hundred thousand footmen (Numbers 11:21) — the arithmetic of unbelief, offered to God as an objection."

"The servants of the king would not put forth their hand (1 Samuel 22:17) — lawful refusal of an unlawful command."
